extractions.extraction_text: retrospective cohort study of patients identified from Mayo Clinic anti-GAD65 samples submitted between 2003 and 2018

323 patients with high-titre (>20 nmol/L in serum) GAD65 antibodies identified from 380,514 submitted samples; after chart review, 108 patients were classified as not having GAD65 neurological autoimmunity and 3 had atypical presentations
study of 212 patients with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity

212 patients; median age at symptom onset 46 years (range 5–83); 77% female; SPSD (N=71), cerebellar ataxia (N=55), epilepsy (N=35), limbic encephalitis (N=7), overlap syndrome (N=44); cognitive impairment (N=38), myelopathy (N=23), brainstem dysfunction (N=22)

SPSD, cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy, and limbic encephalitis designated core manifestations; cognitive impairment, myelopathy, and brainstem dysfunction designated secondary manifestations; cerebellar ataxia and serum GAD65 antibody titre >500 nmol/L predicted poor outcome
Sustained response to immunotherapy ranged from 5/20 (25%) in epilepsy to 32/44 (73%) in SPSD (p=0.002); complete immunotherapy response occurred in 2/142 (1%)
None explicitly stated
evaluation of a large patient cohort with high-titre GAD65 antibodies systematically determined to have GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
Previous reports are limited by small sample sizes or restriction to individual phenotypes, precluding complete disease characterisation
retrospective identification of patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies (>20 nmol/L) detected in the Mayo Clinic Neuroimmunology Laboratory from January 2003 to May 2018 using radioimmunoassay
323 patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies identified from 380,514 samples submitted for anti-GAD65 testing
Patients with non-neurological presentations or more likely alternative diagnoses were excluded from study analysis and summarized separately
Patients with non-neurological presentations or alternative diagnoses were excluded, potentially limiting generalizability

Patients with no more likely alternative diagnosis but an atypical presentation for GAD65 neurological autoimmunity were excluded from study analysis but described separately; remaining patients classified as having GAD65 neurological autoimmunity; data extracted from EMRs for analysis

extractions.extraction_text: Patients with SPSD were classified as classical SPSD, partial SPSD, or SPSD with prominent exaggerated startle; LE was defined as medial temporal lobe T2-hyperintensity with subacute disease onset of less than 3 months; cognitive impairment was diagnosed by the treating physician based on the Kokmen short test of mental status and/or formal neuropsychometric testing
Electroencephalography for epilepsy was frequently gathered, but an abnormal electrophysiological study was not required for diagnosis given imperfect test clinical specificity

Response to immunotherapy (corticosteroids, intravenous IG, plasma exchange, rituximab, cyclophosphamide and/or autologous stem cell transplantation) was classified as no response, partial response, near-complete response, or complete response, as well as sustained (benefit persisting >3 months) or non-sustained, based on review of treating physician’s documentation

Statistical analyses were performed using JMP Pro V .14.1.0; continuous and categorical variables were reported as median (range) and number (percentage), respectively; differences across multiple groups were assessed by Kruskal-Wallis, Pearson’s χ2 or Fisher’s exact test; associations with poor outcome explored by univariate and multivariate logistic regression; two-sided p<0.05 considered significant; no adjustment for multiple comparisons
One in three patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies were classified as not having GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
study analysis of 323 patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies

323 patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies; 37 (11%) had non-neurological presentations and were excluded; 71 (22%) had more likely alternative diagnoses and were excluded; 3 (1%) had atypical presentations and were excluded; 212 (66%) classified as having GAD65 neurological autoimmunity

Median serum anti-GAD65 titre was significantly lower in patients with more likely alternative diagnoses compared with those with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity (149 nmol/L vs 534 nmol/L, p<0.0001); titre was not significantly different compared with patients with non-neurological presentations
SPSD, cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy without LE, and LE could all occur in isolation and were designated core manifestations of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
Patients with two or more core disease manifestations were designated overlap syndromes, except for LE and epilepsy (all patients with LE had seizures)
No patient had cognitive impairment, myelopathy or brainstem dysfunction reported in isolation; these were designated secondary manifestations of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
study of 212 patients with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity

212 patients; median age of symptom onset 46 years (range 5–83); 77% female; 59% had concurrent systemic autoimmunity including thyroid disease (34%), T1DM (30%), and pernicious anaemia (19%); 4% had cancer within 5 years of symptom onset

SPSD was the most common core manifestation, reported in 107/212 (50%); among SPSD cases, 68% had classical SPSD, 28% partial SPSD, and 4% SPSD with exaggerated startle response; electrophysiological findings supportive of SPSD were reported in 52/70 (74%)
spasms (93/107, 87%), gait dysfunction attributed to SPSD (85/107, 79%), and hyperlordosis (49/107, 46%)
Cerebellar ataxia was reported in 91/212 (43%) and often affected gait
Gait ataxia was most frequently documented (76/91, 84%), followed by limb ataxia (63/91, 69%) and ataxic dysarthria (47/91, 52%)
On brain MRI, cerebellar atrophy was observed in 24/91 (26%); no patient had cerebellar T2-hyperintensity or gadolinium enhancement indicative of cerebellitis
A diagnosis of cancer within 5 years of symptom onset was reported in 9/212 (4%), ranging from 0/71 (0%) in SPSD to 6/55 (11%) in cerebellar ataxia
Epilepsy with or without limbic encephalitis was reported in 62/212 (29%)
Seizures were focal-onset in 56/62 (90%) and unknown-onset in 6/62 (10%)
Seizures most often localized to the medial temporal lobe (35/56, 63%)
Seizures were medically refractory in the majority (42/57, 74%)

Medically refractory epilepsy was significantly more frequent among patients with epilepsy in isolation evaluated for seizure management (34/39, 87%) compared with patients with epilepsy as part of an overlap syndrome (8/18, 44%) (p=0.0007)
The most common neuroimaging finding prompting consideration of epilepsy surgery was mesial temporal sclerosis (9/62, 15%)
Eight of 62 patients (13%) underwent epilepsy surgery (unilateral anterior temporal lobectomy, 7 patients; unilateral anterolateral temporal/frontal lobe resections, 1 patient)
Epilepsy surgery uniformly revealed gliosis and did not usually result in seizure freedom

Neuropathological data was available for 5/8 patients, all had gliosis; 2 of 5 had pathological evidence of chronic inflammation (mild leptomeningeal, focal superficial cortical and perivascular chronic inflammation in 1 patient; 'patchy chronic inflammation' in 1 patient); no alternative aetiology for seizures was reported

At last follow-up after surgery, 2 of 8 (25%) obtained seizure freedom; one patient had focal seizures with preserved awareness up to 9 months after surgery that ceased with intravenous IG over two further years of follow-up; one patient had focal seizures with impaired awareness up to ten years after surgery that ceased with addition of clobazam over two further years

Characteristics of 212 patients with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity: 212 total; 71 with stiff-person spectrum disorders (SPSD); 55 with cerebellar ataxia; 35 with epilepsy; 7 with limbic encephalitis (LE); 44 with overlap syndromes
Median age at symptom onset 46 years (range 5–83); Female 163/212 (77%); Caucasian 157/196 (80%)
Median total symptom duration 76 months (range 3–636)
Systemic autoimmunity 125/212 (59%); T1DM 63/212 (30%); Thyroid disease 72/212 (34%); Pernicious anaemia 40/212 (19%); Other 21/212 (10%)
Cancer diagnosed within 5 years of symptom onset 9/212 (4%)
Median serum anti-GAD65 titre 534 nmol/L (range 20.1–7558)
Median CSF anti-GAD65 titre 10 nmol/L (range 0.1–274)
CSF pleocytosis in 15/127 (12%) patients; CSF-specific OCB in 46/114 (40%) patients; elevated CSF protein in 78/122 (64%) patients; elevated CSF IgG index in 10/108 (9%) patients

3 patients had glycine receptor α1 subunit-specific antibodies (two SPSD, 1 overlap of SPSD, cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy); 1 patient with epilepsy had collapsin response-mediator protein 5 antibodies (diagnosed with thymoma, not classified as LE); 1 patient with epilepsy had a clinicoradiographic presentation concerning for GABA type A antibodies but confirmatory testing was not performed
Confirmatory testing for GABA type A antibodies was not performed in one patient
Of patients with overlap syndromes, SPSD was reported in 36/44, cerebellar ataxia in 36/44, epilepsy without LE in 17/44, and LE in 3/44
Other systemic autoimmunity includes adrenal insufficiency, vitiligo and coeliac disease

Cancers diagnosed included thyroid cancer (4: 2 papillary thyroid cancer, 2 not otherwise specified), breast cancer (3: 1 ductal carcinoma, 2 not otherwise specified), lung cancer (3: 1 large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, 1 small cell lung cancer, 1 bronchioalveolar carcinoma), and thymoma (1). Two patients had both breast and thyroid cancer diagnosed

Seven of 9 patients had a cancer diagnosed within 2 years of symptom onset, while the remaining two patients had cancer diagnosed 2–5 years from symptom onset (one thyroid cancer not otherwise specified, 1 breast cancer not otherwise specified)
Testing for anti-GAD65 in CSF was performed in 93/212 patients
Not explicitly stated
Patients stratified by core disease manifestation including epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia, and SPSD; age at symptom onset ranged from 5 to 83 years across groups

Median age at symptom onset ranged from 24 years (range 5–56) in epilepsy to 59 years (range 14–83) in cerebellar ataxia (p<0.0001); in overlap syndromes, median age ranged from 33 years (range 11–60) for epilepsy onset to 53 years for cerebellar ataxia (range 26–69) and SPSD onset (range 19–70) (p<0.0001); median total symptom duration ranged from 42 months (range 3–171) in cerebellar ataxia to 137 months (range 3–552) in epilepsy (p<0.0001)
Six patients continued to have disabling seizures after surgery
Not explicitly stated
Median serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) anti-GAD65 titre did not differ significantly across core manifestations of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity

Patients with epilepsy had the lowest median CSF anti-GAD65 titre (2.5 nmol/L) and the lowest frequency of elevated CSF IgG index (0/22, 0%) among core disease manifestations, but differences were not statistically significant (p=0.10 and p=0.17)
On MRI, medial temporal lobe T2-hyperintensity compatible with limbic encephalitis (LE) was seen in 10/62 (16%) patients
62 patients assessed by MRI for limbic encephalitis
Among LE patients, only 1/10 (10%) were assessed within 3 months of disease onset, and 3/10 (30%) were assessed more than 1 year after disease onset for management of LE sequelae
212 patients with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
Cognitive impairment was reported in 38/212 (18%), predominantly short-term memory in 29/38 (76%), working memory/attention in 6/38 (16%), and verbal fluency/expressive language in 3/38 (8%)
Myelopathy was reported in 23/212 (11%), with upper motor neuron signs in 19/23 (83%), pyramidal weakness in 14/23 (61%), and bowel/bladder dysfunction in 4/23 (17%)
No patient had spinal cord T2-hyperintensity or gadolinium enhancement indicative of myelitis

Brainstem dysfunction was reported in 22/212 (10%) based on oculomotor findings: vertical misalignment in 11/22 (50%), horizontal misalignment in 7/22 (32%), and conjugate ophthalmoparesis in 4/22 (18%)
No patient had brainstem T2-hyperintensity or gadolinium enhancement indicative of brainstem encephalitis

Secondary disease manifestations clustered with specific core disease manifestations: cognitive impairment with epilepsy/LE (N=30/38, 79%), myelopathy with SPSD (N=18/23, 78%), and brainstem dysfunction with cerebellar ataxia (N=20/22, 91%)

Three patients had high-titre GAD65 antibodies but atypical presentations for GAD65 neurological autoimmunity; all had unilateral hyperkinetic movement disorders (dystonia, 2 patients; chorea, 1 patient)

One patient with right lower extremity dystonia received intravenous IG and reported 90% improvement confirmed by the treating physician; dystonia recurred seven to 8 weeks after intravenous IG was discontinued due to intolerability
Immunotherapy usage (corticosteroids, intravenous IG, PLEX, rituximab and cyclophosphamide) was not significantly different across core disease manifestations

Significant overlap of core manifestations (stiff-person spectrum disorder, cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy, limbic encephalitis) and secondary manifestations (myelopathy, brainstem dysfunction, cognitive impairment) of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity was shown in a chord diagram
Corticosteroid usage was infrequent in SPSD (7/44, 16%), the majority received intravenous IG (38/44, 86%)
Median time from symptom onset to first immunotherapy ranged from 5 months (range: 1–22 months) in LE to 50.5 months (range: 1–324 months) in epilepsy
Number of patients with sustained response to immunotherapy ranged from 5/20 (25%) in epilepsy to 32/44 (73%) in SPSD
Complete response to immunotherapy was rare; reported in only 2/142 (1%) patients
212 patients with GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
Presence of cerebellar ataxia and serum GAD65 antibody titre >500 nmol/L predicted poor outcome

Logistic regression analysis revealed that mRS >2 at first Mayo Clinic evaluation, cerebellar ataxia and serum GAD65 antibody titre >500 nmol/L were independent predictors of poor outcome (mRS >2) at last clinical follow-up
systematic review of all Mayo Clinic patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies identified in Neuroimmunology Laboratory over a 15-year period
SPSD, cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy, and LE were core disease manifestations

SPSD was usually classical in presentation; cerebellar ataxia most often impacted gait, with limb and speech ataxia also commonly reported; seizures in epilepsy typically originated from the temporal lobe; three patients had musicogenic epilepsy
Immunotherapy responsiveness differed significantly across core disease manifestations; SPSD was most likely to respond, epilepsy was least responsive
Serum GAD65 antibody titre >500 nmol/L and cerebellar ataxia independently predicted poor outcome; mRS >2 at first Mayo Clinic evaluation also independently predicted poor outcome
The external validity of the mRS >2 finding to other centres requires further study
primarily outpatient tertiary care setting study

LE was least-represented in the cohort; cancer diagnosed within 5 years of symptom onset occurred in 9 of 212 patients (4%)
Referral bias may skew toward more severe epilepsy; patients with severe LE presentations might have been less likely to travel to the facility

Acute immunotherapies used included corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange, rituximab, cyclophosphamide and/or autologous stem cell transplantation; frequency stratified by core disease manifestation is reported in table 3
Second-line acute immunotherapy refers to use of rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide among patients who received acute immunotherapy

Maintenance immunotherapies used for chronic immunomodulation included mycophenolate mofetil (n=37), azathioprine (n=27), intravenous IG (n=27), rituximab (n=19), corticosteroids (n=7), methotrexate (n=2), tacrolimus (n=1) and sirolimus (n=1)
Cognitive impairment was typically amnestic in keeping with medial temporal lobe dysfunction, given the high rate of co-occurrence with temporal lobe epilepsy and LE
Myelopathic findings were most often reported in SPSD and usually manifested as UMN findings (brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses, mild UMN pattern of weakness)
Frequent coexistence of brainstem dysfunction with cerebellar ataxia on the basis of oculomotor findings could reflect more diffuse posterior fossa inflammation (‘rhombencephalitis’) in some patients
Three patients had hyperkinetic movement disorders, suggesting this phenotype may be part of the spectrum of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity
Given the paucity of cases, thorough evaluation for other causes of a hyperkinetic movement disorder in a patient with high-titre GAD65 antibodies is recommended
On review of immunotherapy usage across core disease manifestations, only corticosteroid usage differed significantly
Rates of sustained response to immunotherapy ranged from 73% in SPSD to only 25% in epilepsy

Due to the retrospective nature of this study we were not able to implement standardised measures of disease severity when monitoring responses to immunotherapy; classification of response was based on the Mayo Clinic treating physician’s documentation, which has an element of subjectivity

High prevalence of epilepsy among patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies; inflammation reported neuropathologically in 2 of 5 patients who underwent epilepsy surgery; trend toward lower median CSF anti-GAD65 titre and less frequent elevated CSF IgG index compared with other core disease manifestations
Poor response to immunotherapy in patients with epilepsy and high-titre GAD65 antibodies; delay to immunotherapy likely contributes to lack of immunotherapy-responsiveness

serum GAD65 antibody titre >500 nmol/L and cerebellar ataxia were independent predictors of poor outcome (mRS >2)
Clinical reporting of GAD65 antibodies in the Mayo Clinic Neuroimmunology Laboratory is based only on RIA, and so confirmation of high-titre GAD65 antibodies by a second assay was not performed

Reporting of anti-GAD65 by TIIF is not routinely done, and serum positivity for anti-GAD65 by TIIF may occur in patients without GAD65 neurological autoimmunity, highlighting the challenge in determining what test methodology or cut-off best defines a clinically relevant high-titre GAD65 antibody result.

Implementation of other test methodologies such as ELISA, immunoblot or cell-based assay to detect high-titre GAD65 antibodies in some laboratories has created the need for assay comparison studies, which is an area of active investigation.
High-titre GAD65 antibodies in serum are best viewed as necessary, but not sufficient for a diagnosis of GAD65 neurological autoimmunity.
The presence of anti-GAD65 in CSF supports an autoimmune aetiology in the appropriate clinical context.

Calculation of intrathecal anti-GAD65 synthesis is not performed in our testing laboratory and was not required for study inclusion; it is not yet in widespread use and systematic evaluation of its diagnostic utility in clinical practice is required
Lack of a diagnostic gold standard for GAD65 neurological autoimmunity independent of GAD65 antibody testing

One-third of patients with high-titre GAD65 antibodies were excluded prior to study analysis because they were classified as not having GAD65 neurological autoimmunity due to non-neurological presentations
Rigorous clinical evaluation to rule out alternative diagnoses in patients with atypical features remains prudent

High number of excluded patients could reflect referral bias at specialised tertiary care centre enriched with atypical presentations for GAD65 neurological autoimmunity and alternative diagnoses; possible contributory GAD65 autoimmunity in patients with more likely alternative neurological diagnoses
